turns.user: Explain why a cache can speed up repeated reads.
turns.assistant:
**Answer**

A cache keeps a copy of data you already fetched. The next read can use that copy instead of going back to the slow source.

**Why**

The first read is slow because the data may live on a disk or over a network. Those paths take more time than reading from fast memory nearby.

A cache stores the result of that first read in faster storage, often RAM. When you ask for the same data again, the system checks the cache first. A hit means it returns the stored copy right away.

That skips the slow trip to disk or the network. Repeated reads of the same data get much faster because most requests never leave fast memory.

**Example**

You open a web page. The browser saves images and scripts in a cache. Reload the page and those files load from cache instead of downloading again. The page appears faster on the second load.
